## Data to Decisions {#data-to-decisions}

::: {.module-tag}
Module 4
:::

### 🪝 Hook

Imagine you have access to sea level data, reef health maps, and climate projections for your island. Now, imagine sitting across from a local official who has to decide where to invest limited infrastructure funds. What do you actually say?

This is the **last-mile problem** - the gap between what cyberinfrastructure produces and what decision-makers can actually use. Data alone doesn't make decisions. Someone has to translate it, communicate it, and connect it to action. This module is about that gap - and how to bridge it.

**Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)** are climate commitments each country submits under the Paris Agreement — outlining what they plan to do to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. The **Regional Pacific NDC Hub** supports 14 Pacific island nations in developing and implementing these plans, and their website brings together country profiles, climate commitments, and implementation resources in one place.

NDCs are a real example of the last-mile problem in action — they take scientific data and climate projections and translate them into government commitments and policy priorities.

::: {.fieldtrip-box}
**Your task this module:**

Visit the [Regional Pacific NDC Hub](https://pacificndc.org){target="_blank"} and explore resources for your chosen island country.

**What to look for:**

- Does your island country have an NDC profile or resources on the hub?
- What sustainability priorities and climate commitments are highlighted?
- What data or evidence is referenced to support those commitments? (Read some of the documents under the country's profile.)
- How does the language in these documents connect to the CI tools and data you've explored in previous weeks?

If your island country is not one of the 14 Hub member countries, browse the profile of the geographically closest member country and note the similarities and differences.
:::

::: {.resource-link}
📖 **Read more:** [CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5d3799de845604000199cd24/t/6397b363b502ff481fce6baf/1670886246948/CARE%2BPrinciples_One%2BPagers%2BFINAL_Oct_17_2019.pdf){target="_blank"} — approximately 5 pages. Consider how each principle applies to Pacific data governance contexts.
:::

### 📋 Mini Assignment - Stakeholder + CI Pipeline Map

::: {.assignment-box}
**Week 4 Assignment - Stakeholder + CI Pipeline Map**

For your chosen island country and sustainability challenge, produce a structured map/document covering the following five areas. This map becomes the evidence section of your policy brief in Weeks 5 and 6 - so be as specific and honest as you can. Identifying gaps is just as valuable as identifying what exists.

1. **The sustainability problem:** One clear sentence describing the challenge and who is affected.
2. **Key decision-makers:** Who are the 2-3 people or institutions that make decisions about this challenge? (e.g. Ministry of Environment, village council, regional fisheries body)
3. **CI that currently exists:** What data, platforms, or models are already available for this challenge? Reference tools or datasets you've encountered in Weeks 1-3. Research and look for more CI tools that exist online. 
4. **What is missing:** What CI gap most limits good decision-making here? Be specific - not just "more data" but what kind, held by whom, used by whom.
5. **Who is excluded:** Who is affected by this sustainability challenge but left out of the data collection or the decision-making process?

Add your responses to the **Week 4 section of your Pacific CI Portfolio** Google Doc and submit the link in Google Classroom.

[→ Submit Week 4 Assignment in Google Classroom](https://classroom.google.com){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"}
:::
